final_recommendation: The room converged on a labor-only amendment framework: majority-vote panel findings trigger same-day suspension on labor trade flows, with Mexico's 15-day remedy window running in parallel. Labor commits to public endorsement Friday if binding text matches this operational definition; Congress schedules floor vote contingent on labor's statement; business mobilizes swing-district support. Amendment scope explicitly locked to labor enforcement—no reopening of dairy, Chapter 19, or rules of origin.
minority_objections: Business initially resisted timeline uncertainty before amendment text existed, demanding premature Congressional commitment
Canada repeatedly flagged risk that labor amendment could become wedge to reopen dairy/Chapter 19, requiring explicit scope-lock language in operative text
key_conflicts: Automatic vs. conditional suspension: Labor/Congress demanded same-day suspension on panel finding; Mexico initially unclear whether 15-day remedy window preceded or ran parallel to suspension
Scope creep risk: Canada vs. all parties on whether labor amendment could reopen non-labor chapters
Timing coordination: Business wanted public commitment before amendment text existed; Congress/labor refused to move without binding language
key_concessions: Mexico: accepted majority-vote panel findings with no veto on violation declarations, same-day suspension trigger, legal review completed before Wednesday commitment
Labor: accepted 15-day parallel remedy window (not blocking suspension) in exchange for automatic trigger
Congress: agreed to floor vote timeline contingent on labor's public endorsement, not independent review
Business: accepted waiting for Friday text before mobilizing public support, abandoning demand for premature commitment
red_lines: Labor: no ratification if suspension is conditional (remedy-first) rather than automatic (same-day trigger)
Canada: no ratification if amendment scope not explicitly locked to labor-only in operative language
Mexico: no acceptance of U.S. unilateral suspension authority outside joint panel process
Congress: no floor vote without labor's written public endorsement that enforcement 'actually works'
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation risk: no discussion of how same-day suspension executes operationally (customs procedures, tariff schedules, industry notification)
Chapter 20 litigation strategy: trade lawyer confirmed Mexico can challenge finding validity while suspension runs, but no discussion of how prolonged litigation affects enforcement credibility
Domestic Mexican ratification: no participant raised whether Mexico's legislature would accept same-day suspension trigger or view it as sovereignty infringement
Business supply-chain disruption: no discussion of how automatic suspension on labor flows affects just-in-time manufacturing or cross-border value chains
downstream_risk_variables: Labor's Friday public statement becomes binding constraint on Congressional floor vote—any hedging language kills momentum
Mexico's Wednesday legal review must pre-clear both suspension trigger AND scope-lock language—failure on either collapses timeline
Canada's domestic opposition mobilizes if amendment text lacks explicit 'labor-only' operative language, threatening trilateral ratification
Business uncertainty persists until Friday text drops—market narrative remains 'deal at risk' through Thursday
Media narrative shifts from 'stalled talks' to 'enforcement breakthrough' only if all three commitments (Mexico Wednesday, labor Thursday, Congress Friday) execute on schedule
uncertainty_notes: Thursday's draft language remains the critical gate: if labor's text includes any ambiguity on same-day suspension trigger, scope lock, or Chapter 20 stay provisions, Mexico's Wednesday commitment unravels and Congress loses Friday timeline. No participant confirmed whether Mexico's legal team has actually pre-cleared the operational definition (same-day suspension, parallel remedy) or is seeing it for first time Wednesday. Business mobilization on Friday depends entirely on labor's public statement—no fallback if labor hedges on 'this works' language.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress opened with 'I've got the votes to kill this thing or move it, but not as-is'—ratification failure drove every subsequent move, including amendment framework and Friday deadline
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor's demand for same-day automatic suspension (not consultation or remedy-first) was the central constraint that shaped Mexico's commitment, Congress's timeline, and the entire amendment structure
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business conditioned support on timeline certainty and demanded coordinated Friday push, but accepted waiting for binding text—important but not the room's dominant driver
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada repeatedly demanded scope-lock language to prevent dairy reopening and flagged domestic opposition risk, but this was defensive/protective rather than driving the room's direction
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico accepted majority-vote findings and same-day suspension but required parallel remedy window and rejected U.S. unilateral authority—sovereignty was a constraint Mexico managed, not a theme that drove others
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media pushed for coordinated announcements and headline clarity, but participants repeatedly denied premature commitments—media amplified rather than drove the substantive moves
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: The room treated ratification as impossible without amendment ('we're wasting everyone's time' without enforcement mechanism)—stability required reopening, making this a central organizing assumption throughout
